what_it_does: BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms) is a standard set of mathematical operations — adding vectors, multiplying matrices, and so on — that underpin almost all scientific computing and engineering software. These operations are bottlenecked by how fast data can move between memory and the processor (memory bandwidth), not by raw arithmetic speed, so making the processor faster does not help much. This paper proposes doing the math directly inside the memory chip — an approach called processing-in-memory (PIM), where arithmetic units are embedded in or near the memory arrays so data does not need to travel over the slow bus to the CPU or GPU. The design is built on non-volatile memory (NVM — a type of storage that retains data without power, such as flash or phase-change memory), and it supports high-precision floating-point arithmetic (unlike many PIM proposals that only handle integers or low precision). A configurable set of data-movement patterns (dataflows) lets the same hardware efficiently serve all three levels of BLAS — simple vector operations (level 1), matrix-vector products (level 2), and matrix-matrix products (level 3 — the most compute-intensive). The claimed result is that memory-bound operations run entirely inside memory, while even compute-bound operations benefit from PIM's high internal parallelism, though quantitative results are not available from the abstract.
